questions.scenario: The interest job ran on 31 October for business date 30 October and failed. It's rerun with businessDate=2026-10-30.
questions.question: What does Spring Batch do?
options: Starts a new job instance from the first account
Deletes the first run's postings and starts again
Creates a new execution of the same instance and restarts from the last committed chunk
questions.explanation: The identifying parameters name the instance; a failed instance is restarted using the saved reader position.

questions.scenario: The job processes chunks of 100 and fails on the 457th account.
questions.question: What has been committed?
options: Nothing: the whole job rolls back
questions.explanation: Each chunk is one transaction; the failing chunk rolls back and earlier ones stay committed.

questions.scenario: A reader selects accounts without an ORDER BY.
questions.question: Why is this a problem for restarts?
options: The saved position may point at different rows next time, so a restart can skip or repeat accounts
questions.explanation: Restart relies on a stable sort order, ideally on a unique key.

questions.scenario: The writer uses INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (account_id, business_date) DO NOTHING.
questions.question: What does this protect against?
options: Posting interest twice for the same account and day, even if a chunk were written again
questions.explanation: An idempotent writer is the second line of defence after the saved reader position.

questions.scenario: A developer uses LocalDate.now() inside the interest processor.
questions.question: What goes wrong?
options: A rerun on a later day posts interest for the wrong date; pass the business date as a job parameter
questions.explanation: Batch jobs work on a business date, which can differ from the calendar date of the run.

questions.scenario: The job fails at 1 a.m. in Kubernetes.
questions.question: How does the scheduler know?
options: The process exits with a non-zero code
It doesn't; someone checks in the morning
questions.explanation: Spring Boot exits with the job's status (the starter's failed run exits with code 5); schedulers act on exit codes.

questions.scenario: An account has corrupt data and fails processing every time.
questions.question: What is the responsible way to keep the run going?
options: Catch the exception and return null silently
Skip it with a limit and write each skipped account to an exceptions report operations must clear
questions.explanation: Skipping is a business decision; every skip must be visible and followed up.

questions.scenario: The interest job for 1,000,000 accounts takes too long.
questions.question: Which change speeds it up while keeping restarts reliable?
options: Partition the accounts into ranges, each a worker step that restarts independently
Load all accounts into memory first
questions.explanation: Partitioning parallelises the work; each partition keeps its own restart state.
